newsitem.title: ITALY: Shocked Italy to probe alleged Somalia horrors.
newsitem.headline: Shocked Italy to probe alleged Somalia horrors.

text.p: Italy said on Friday it would launch a full inquiry into allegations that troops on a peacekeeping mission to Somalia tortured, sexually assaulted and killed unarmed Somalis.
A defence ministry statement said a joint commission of magistrates and military officers would investigate the allegations reported in the news magazine Panorama.
The inquiry would look beyond the alleged episodes "to ascertain the scale and extent of deviant phenomena contrary to military honour in the course of the entire operation", it said.

The Panorama reports, launched last week with allegations of torture of Somalis by a former soldier, have shocked Italians and embarrassed the military. Italy sent troops to Somalia in late 1992 as part of a U.S-led humanitarian mission.
President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro on Friday called a meeting for next Wednesday of Italy's Supreme Defence Council, a body which convenes only rarely.

Though a presidential office statement made no mention of the Somalia scandal, it said the council would hear a report from defence chief Admiral Guido Venturoni on "international missions by the Italian armed forces".
The reports of abuse have broken as Italy seeks to raise its international profile through leadership of a multinational security force deployed in Albania since April.
Panorama carried fresh reports of alleged abuses in its latest edition on Friday, backed by photographs and interviews with two more former soldiers.

One series of photographs showed what Panorama said was the sadistic sexual assault of a young Somali woman at an Italian checkpoint, codenamed "Demon", on the road from Mogadishu to Balad in late November 1993.
The photographs, taken by an ex-member of the elite Folgore paratroop division, appeared to show the woman tied by her ankles to an armoured car and in a state of undress.

"She was screaming and struggling, not so much because of the physical pain, perhaps, but because she didn't want it to happen," the former soldier who took the photographs, named only as Stefano, told Panorama.

Another ex-soldier, former fusilier Benedetto Bertini, told Panorama that he believed Italian troops had killed at least six unarmed Somali civilians in a jeep near Belet Huen on the Somali border with Ethiopia.
"We were in a column. We received a radio message saying: 'Don't worry if you hear shots. We're target-shooting Somalis'," he was quoted as saying.
He said that when his patrol reached the scene, the jeep had been destroyed with rifle grenades and its occupants lay dead.
"We were told (by our instructors) that we shouldn't treat Somalis like human beings...The order was: 'If in doubt, fire' even if they were women and children," Bertini said.
The ill-fated multinational mission to Somalia, a former Italian colony, was designed to help distribute food around the country in the Horn of Africa.
It soon disintegrated into a military campaign against fugitive warlord Mohamed Farah Aideed. Three Italian peacekeepers were killed in an ambush in July, 1993.

Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta said authorities would show no leniency to soldiers involved in what he called "these horrendous acts", nor to any superior officers who failed to exercise proper control.
"The honour of the armed forces is at stake and this must be cleared up fully and fast," he told reporters.
